newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Aid agencies to reduce staff in Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Aid agencies to reduce staff in Kabul.

text.p: Aid agencies in Kabul have decided to cut the number of their international staff as the front line between warring factions in Afghanistan gets nearer to the capital.
Opposition forces under their commander Ahmed Shah Masood have made significant advances towards Kabul from the north over the past few days.
The front line is now less than 40 miles (64 km) away.

"It is a voluntary staff reduction because we don't know what Masood is going to do next. It means that if we do come to an evacuation there will be less people to evacuate," Ross Everson, of the aid agency umbrella body Agency Coordinating Body for Afghan Relief, said on Tuesday.
Everson said only 14 of more than 120 international aid staff would be leaving Kabul by road on Wednesday.
"In an emergency the airport will be closed, as will most of the roads, and we don't have enough four-wheel-drives to get everybody out," he said.
"If the situation deteriorates further, we will be asking more people to leave."
In the past, most aid agency personnel movements have been on Red Cross or United Nations planes through Kabul airport.
Both agencies temporarily suspended flights after the airport became the target of a number of recent opposition air attacks.
An air raid on Sunday afternoon missed the airport and hit a residential area, killing seven people and wounding 12. The United Nations has asked the opposition to avoid targeting civilian areas.
The United Nations said on Tuesday night that it was not intending to pull out any international staff immediately.
On Saturday night, the opposition alliance managed to push the Taleban out of the town of Charikar (40 miles, 64 km north of Kabul) and the nearby Bagram air base.
The Taleban have dug in on new front lines south of Charikar and overlooking the air base, but there is uncertainty in Kabul that they can hold the resurgent opposition forces.
The Taleban appear to have held off an attack on two fronts on Tuesday morning, but many observers believe that they have been weakened by a string of recent defeats at the hands of the opposition.
The purist Islamic Taleban have been under continuous pressure since they briefly captured most of the opposition-held north of the country in May.
But they still control most of Afghanistan, including the capital, and are the most formidable single force in the country.
